newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament claims art seized from Germany.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament claims art seized from Germany.

text.p: The Russian parliament approved a draft law on Wednesday claiming ownership of works of art seized from Nazi Germany during World War Two, including treasures from ancient Troy and priceless paintings by Henri Matisse.
The bill, which would turn art valuables snatched by the Soviet Union during World War Two into Russian property, was passed unopposed by the Federation Council, parliament's upper chamber.
In the vote, 140 deputies supported the draft and one abstained. None opposed the legislation, which had already been approved by the lower house.
President Boris Yeltsin must sign the law before it comes into force, but it has been criticised by both the Russian and German governments,
Russian deputy culture minister Mikhail Shvydkoi urged Yeltsin not to sign.
"The government and the culture ministry consider that the art problems cannot be solved by a law which would harm Russia's position in ongoing negotiations," he told reporters.
Germany has demanded the return of the artefacts and has appealed to Yeltsin for help several times.
But many Russians view the treasures as compensation for Russian works of art destroyed by the Nazis and the wartime suffering of the Soviet Union.
The artworks were seized by Soviet soldiers at the end of World War Two from museums and private homes in Germany, its wartime allies and countries occupied by Nazi forces.

The row centres on around 200,000 works of art, including priceless paintings by Matisse, Francisco de Goya and Paul Cezanne, some three km (two miles) of archive documents and about two million books.

The booty also includes a priceless collection of Trojan gold, unearthed by German archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann in 1873. Schliemann claimed his find belonged to King Priam, the king of the ancient Greek city of Troy featured in Homer's epic poem "The Iliad".
The draft law would also give former Soviet republics, including the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, the right to claim back artworks brought to Russia.

Germany has argued that Russia is obliged under two existing treaties to hand the artworks back, but German experts said recently there was still a chance of a compromise even after Russian parliament approved the law.
"Negotiations are under way and there are a couple of ideas (for compromise)," said one German expert close to the talks.
He gave no details but indicated Germany might be ready to leave some artefacts in Russia and become involved in a series of Russian cultural projects as a show of political goodwill.
Last July, the Federation Council rejected a similar draft law, saying approval would harm international relations.
